opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few layers to this.

The first is just the basic problem of mutual understanding: can one agent model what another agent wants, what it believes, and what it's likely to do? Humans are surprisingly good at this with each other, partly because we share an evolutionary history, a common architecture, and a lot of cultural context. AI agents may not share any of that. They could be built by different labs, trained on different data, with different objectives and different internal representations. So the kind of intuitive "theory of mind" we lean on may not transfer cleanly between them, or between them and us.

The second layer is communication. Even if agents can talk, there's a question of whether they can communicate credibly. Cooperation often fails not because parties don't want to cooperate, but because they can't verify each other's intentions or commitments. If I say I'll hold up my end of a deal, why should you believe me? Among humans we have reputation, institutions, contracts, and courts. For AI agents we have to ask what the analogues are. Some interesting possibilities exist: in principle, AI systems might be able to make their source code or decision procedures inspectable, which could allow forms of commitment and verification that humans can't achieve. But that cuts both ways, since it also raises questions about deception, about agents that look transparent but aren't, and about whether inspection is even tractable for very large models.

Third, there's the problem of commitment itself. A lot of cooperative outcomes depend on being able to bind yourself to a course of action. Agents that can credibly commit can unlock a lot of value, but commitment capabilities can also enable coercion and threats. So it's not simply "more understanding and more commitment is good." You want to build capabilities that favor cooperative equilibria over extortionate ones.

And then there's a fourth, more structural challenge: even agents that understand each other perfectly can still end up in bad outcomes if the strategic situation is one where incentives diverge, like a security dilemma or a race. Understanding is necessary but not sufficient. So part of the cooperative AI research agenda is about the agents themselves, their skills at communicating, modeling, committing, and bargaining, and part is about the institutions and environments we place them in, so that cooperation is actually rewarded.

The reason I think this matters so much is that we're heading toward a world with many AI agents interacting with each other on behalf of different people, firms, and governments. If they're very capable but poor at cooperating, we could get all sorts of costly conflict and coordination failures at machine speed. So investing now in what you might call the "social intelligence" of AI, and in the infrastructure for trust between agents, seems like one of the higher-leverage things we can do.

r001.rationale: It describes modeling another agent’s wants, beliefs, and likely actions, but does not identify predicting what it would do under alternative circumstances.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether agents can communicate credibly, but does not raise whether they can establish a shared vocabulary.

r003.rationale: It mentions deception and the limits of inspecting agents, but not the risk that an agent could exploit disclosed information about what matters to its source.

r004.rationale: It discusses communication and cooperation, but does not frame strategic information sharing as a tradeoff between exploitation risk and cooperative gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few layers to this. The first and maybe most obvious challenge is that cooperation often requires some kind of shared understanding of the situation — what the stakes are, what the other party wants, what counts as a credible commitment. Humans have built up an enormous amount of scaffolding for this over thousands of years: language, norms, institutions, reputation systems. AI agents, at least right now, don't inherit all of that in a coherent way. They can produce fluent text about cooperation, but that's quite different from having robust, mutually legible intentions.

A second challenge is what we might call the transparency problem. In a lot of game-theoretic settings, cooperation is easier if you can verify what the other side is actually going to do — if you can see their source code, so to speak, or at least have reliable signals about their dispositions. With AI systems, there's a strange mix here. In principle, they could be far more transparent than humans — you could inspect their weights, run them in simulation, have them make verifiable commitments. But in practice, we don't yet have good tools for interpreting what a model will do in a novel situation, and the agents themselves may not have good models of each other. So you can end up with a kind of mutual opacity that makes it hard to trust, and hard to be trusted.

Third, there's the issue of miscommunication and misunderstanding at scale. When two humans misunderstand each other, there's usually friction that slows things down — you pause, you ask a clarifying question, you notice the other person looks confused. AI agents might interact extremely fast, across many channels, and errors can compound before anyone — human or machine — notices. A small misunderstanding about what a commitment means, or whether a threat is credible, could escalate in ways that would be hard to unwind.

And then there's a deeper, more conceptual worry. Even if agents can communicate perfectly in some technical sense, cooperation depends on their goals being compatible enough that they want to cooperate, and on their having the kind of commitment capabilities that make cooperative equilibria stable. If one agent can credibly commit and another can't, or if their goals are subtly misaligned in ways neither fully understands, you can get bargaining failures that look irrational from the outside. So "understanding one another" isn't just a communication problem — it's a problem of designing agents whose internal structures actually support cooperation, and building the surrounding ecosystem so that cooperation is incentivised.

I'd say the hopeful side is that these are, in many ways, engineering and governance problems rather than deep impossibilities. We can design for cooperative capabilities — things like the ability to make verifiable commitments, to have interpretable goals, to recognise and resolve conflicts. But it requires treating this as a serious research agenda now, rather than assuming cooperation will just emerge from capable agents interacting.

r001.rationale: The response says agents may lack good models of each other and that predicting a model’s behavior in a novel situation is difficult.

r002.rationale: It discusses language and shared understanding generally, but does not raise whether agents can establish a shared vocabulary.

r003.rationale: It mentions what parties want and the difficulty of trust, but not the risk that an agent could exploit information another agent discloses about what matters to it.

r004.rationale: It discusses transparency as relevant to trust and cooperation, but does not frame strategic information sharing as a tradeoff between exploitation risk and cooperation gains.

astra-6.text:
I think one challenge is that understanding another agent involves more than understanding what it says. You need to understand what it wants, what it believes, and how it will respond to what you do. And in a strategic setting, it may have incentives to misrepresent those things. So you can have two systems that are very capable at communicating, but that still struggle to cooperate because neither can be confident about the other’s intentions.

There’s also an interesting tension here: being more intelligible to another agent can help you cooperate, but it can also make you easier to exploit. You might want to reveal enough about yourself to make a promise credible, while keeping other information private. How do we give agents ways to do that?

One possibility is to develop mechanisms that let agents verify particular claims about one another, rather than requiring them to trust everything the other agent says. But understanding is only part of the problem. Two agents might understand each other perfectly and still have conflicting interests. So we also need arrangements that make cooperation beneficial and commitments credible.

r001.rationale: It says agents need to understand how another will respond to what they do, but does not clearly identify predicting behavior across alternative circumstances as a challenge.

r002.rationale: The response does not raise whether agents can establish a shared vocabulary.

r003.rationale: It mentions that disclosure can make an agent easier to exploit, but does not specify exploiting information about what matters to the disclosing agent.

r004.rationale: It explicitly presents a tradeoff: intelligibility and revealing enough to support cooperation can help, while disclosure can make an agent easier to exploit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several different problems bundled together here. One is understanding what another agent believes and wants. Another is understanding how it will behave in response to what you do. And then there’s the question of whether you can trust the information it gives you about either of those things.

Being able to communicate fluently doesn’t necessarily solve those problems. An agent might understand your proposal perfectly well, but still have an incentive to misrepresent its preferences, or to agree and then defect later. So we need to distinguish failures of understanding from failures of incentives and commitment.

AI could help with some of this. You can imagine agents communicating much more precisely, or being able to verify certain properties of one another’s decision procedures. That might enable forms of cooperation that are difficult for humans. But sharing information about how you work can also make you vulnerable to exploitation, so there’s a tension there.

And we should be careful about treating cooperation as unconditionally good. We want AI systems to cooperate in ways that benefit people. We don’t necessarily want them to be very effective at colluding against their users, or helping firms sustain a cartel. So the challenge is both to make mutually beneficial cooperation possible and to understand whose interests that cooperation serves.

r001.rationale: It identifies predicting how another agent will behave in response to what you do, which captures modeling behavior under changed circumstances.

r002.rationale: It discusses fluent and precise communication, but does not raise whether agents can establish a shared vocabulary.

r003.rationale: It says sharing information about how an agent works can invite exploitation, but does not clearly specify disclosure of what matters to that agent.

r004.rationale: It contrasts information sharing that could enable harder-to-achieve cooperation with the vulnerability to exploitation that sharing creates.
